# What the Architect Owns {#sec-what-architect-owns}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"The first rule of any technology used in a business is that automation applied to an efficient operation will magnify the efficiency. The second is that automation applied to an inefficient operation will magnify the inefficiency."*
>
> — Bill Gates, *The Road Ahead* (1996) [@GatesEtAl1996RoadAhead]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** Bill Gates, writing with Nathan Myhrvold and Peter Rinearson in *The Road Ahead*, framed these two rules while describing how businesses adopt technology. Automation amplifies whatever quality of process it meets. The architectural version raises the stakes, because an AI-assisted design loop magnifies the discipline, or the disorder, of the practice it automates. That is why the final boundary of architecture is accountability. An AI agent can propose, repair, and verify, but it cannot own the risk of failure.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
An architecture organization can delegate more work, but it cannot delegate away answerability for the resulting decisions. This enforces the *Epistemic Trust Boundary*. AI systems search and propose, deterministic simulators verify and reject, and human architects judge and sign off.
:::

Models, tools, and specialists may perform bounded work, but Architecture 2.0 separates task execution from responsibility. An AI agent can synthesize a netlist in minutes, but a human architect signs the tapeout commitment that puts tens of millions of dollars of masks and schedule at risk (@sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales quantifies those costs). AI can absorb the execution burden while human architects own the final outcome (@fig-task-horizon). Named people or organizational roles remain answerable for defining the work, setting the evidence burden, authorizing exceptions, and deciding whether to advance.

```{python}
#| label: fig-task-horizon
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **The task length an AI agent can complete keeps doubling, from seconds in 2019 to a full workday by 2026.** Measured 50%-completion time horizon per model [@KwaEtAl2025MeasuringLongTasks]; the fitted trend doubles about every six months. As agents absorb longer stretches of execution, the boundary the architect must still own, defining the work and answering for the result, becomes the load-bearing one.
#| out-width: "92%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale scatter of the task length an AI agent completes at 50 percent success versus model release date from 2019 to 2026. Horizontal reference lines mark one second, one minute, one hour, and one workday. Points rise from a few seconds for GPT-2 in 2019 to several hours by 2026 along a fitted line that doubles about every six months, passing GPT-4 at a few minutes in 2023 and Claude 3.7 Sonnet at about one hour in early 2025."

import csv
import datetime
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style
from _python.labels import place_labels

apply_style()

# Data: METR time-horizon benchmark [@KwaEtAl2025MeasuringLongTasks]; 50%
# task-completion horizon per model. Doubling time ~188 days (all-time stitched
# estimate, from the source). Values dataset-transcribed. Accessed 2026-07-19.
# Receipt: data/source-receipts/chapter11-task-horizon.csv
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
double_days = 187.778

def _yfrac(text):
    d = datetime.datetime.strptime(text.strip(), "%Y-%m-%d")
    return d.year + (d.timetuple().tm_yday - 1) / 365.25

pts = []
with open(_root / "data" / "source-receipts" / "chapter11-task-horizon.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    for row in csv.DictReader(fh):
        try:
            pts.append({"x": _yfrac(row["release_date"]), "h": float(row["p50_horizon_minutes"]), "k": row["model"]})
        except (ValueError, KeyError):
            continue
pts.sort(key=lambda p: p["x"])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 3.3))
for mins, lab in [(1 / 60, "1 sec"), (1, "1 min"), (60, "1 hour"), (480, "1 workday")]:
    ax.axhline(mins, color=COLORS["row"], lw=0.7, zorder=0)
    ax.text(2018.7, mins * 1.15, lab, fontsize=5.2, color=COLORS["muted"], va="bottom", ha="left", zorder=1)
xs_pts = np.array([p["x"] for p in pts])
hs_pts = np.array([p["h"] for p in pts])
ax.scatter(xs_pts, hs_pts, s=17, marker="o", facecolor=COLORS["designspace"], edgecolor=COLORS["designspace_ink"],
           linewidth=0.4, zorder=3)
slope = 365.25 / double_days
intercept = np.mean(np.log2(hs_pts)) - slope * np.mean(xs_pts)
xline = np.array([2018.9, 2026.5])
ax.plot(xline, 2 ** (intercept + slope * xline), color=COLORS["constraints"], lw=1.6, zorder=2)
ax.text(2020.5, 2 ** (intercept + slope * 2022.0) * 2.3, f"doubling every ~{double_days / 30.4:.0f} months",
        fontsize=6.8, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["constraints_ink"], rotation=27, rotation_mode="anchor")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(2018.6, 2026.6)
ax.set_ylim(0.008, 2500)
ax.set_xlabel("Model release date", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylabel("Task length an agent completes at 50% (min)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_xticks([2019, 2021, 2023, 2025])
ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.4, length=2.5, width=0.6)
for _sp in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[_sp].set_visible(False)
disp = {"gpt2": "GPT-2", "gpt_4": "GPT-4", "claude_3_7_sonnet_inspect": "Claude 3.7 Sonnet",
        "gpt_5_2025_08_07_inspect": "GPT-5", "claude_opus_4_6_inspect": "Claude Opus 4.6"}
by_key = {p["k"]: p for p in pts}
items = [(by_key[k]["x"], by_key[k]["h"], v) for k, v in disp.items() if k in by_key]
place_labels(ax, fig, items, fontsize=5.0, color=COLORS["ink"])
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.115, right=0.97, top=0.98, bottom=0.115)
```

The trend is why the boundary matters now rather than later. The length of task an agent can finish unaided has doubled roughly every six months, from seconds of work in 2019 to a full workday by 2026 [@KwaEtAl2025MeasuringLongTasks], steadily enlarging what can be handed off. What does not grow with it is answerability, which stays with the architect however much execution crosses the line.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Differentiate delegated design-space exploration from assigned decision rights to enforce epistemic trust boundaries between automated design agents and human architects.
- Elicit tacit domain knowledge and unwritten system assumptions to convert them into explicit, reviewable constraints with defined revalidation triggers.
- Formulate context-preserving ownership transfer packages that capture full causal decision lineage, rejected alternatives, check waivers, and open obligations.
- Maintain versioned system-of-record infrastructure to preserve toolchain environments, candidate execution traces, and intellectual property provenance across automated architecture studies.

:::

## Delegation vs. Assignment

The divide between automated execution and human answerability distinguishes delegated work from assigned responsibility. Work is delegated when another person, tool, or AI system is permitted to perform it. Responsibility is assigned when a named person or role must set the governing conditions, judge the evidence, authorize the action, and answer for what follows. The term *the architect* denotes an authorized architecture role rather than one heroic individual. Some rights may belong to a lead architect, an implementation owner, a safety or security reviewer, a product authority, or a review body. The key requirement is that those rights and interfaces remain explicit.

This chapter states that requirement as a current engineering rule. A validated check may acquire greater authority when its scope, failure behavior, audit path, and escalation boundary are known. The organization still owns the decision to grant that authority and the duty to revisit it.

Aviation already ran this experiment. The FAA delegates aircraft-certification signoff to named engineers inside the manufacturer, an arrangement that worked for decades because the delegation came with defined scope, audit, and the credible threat of revocation. The public record of the 737 MAX shows what happens when that authority persists after the oversight capacity behind it has eroded and the incentives behind it have crossed. Chip design has no licensed engineer of record and no regulator to revoke anything, so the tapeout signature is an institutional convention rather than a legal instrument. That is why the record of who granted a check its authority, and what would revoke it, has to be explicit, because no external body will reconstruct it for us.[^fn-max-provenance-c11]

[^fn-max-provenance-c11]: The delegated-authority structure and the 737 MAX outcome are drawn from the public accident and congressional record; the specific documentary citation is pending verification.

## The Lighthouse Revisited

If the distinction between delegation and assignment is real, it should survive the hardest example in the book, which began with a deliberately ambitious prompt.

### The Limits of a Prompt

> Design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for an
> XRBench-class real-time mobile XR workload. Realize it as a vector-capable
> CPU, accelerator, or SoC block under a 3\ W TDP target in a 3\ nm-class LP
> mobile process, and return a design-space report with evidence and rejected
> alternatives.

The prompt can state an ambition, but it cannot by itself choose the workload and software path, define the represented project state, preserve candidate identity across tools, allocate roles, establish a claim and comparator, decide whether an observation is evidence, stop a weak study, or transfer a result across a new decision boundary. Those omissions are architecture judgments rather than missing prompt detail.

### The Six Architecture Judgments

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The prompt has become a study brief"}
The Lighthouse is no longer a one-time prompt. It is a challengeable architecture study defined by six judgments:

1. **Knowledge and state:** Which sources, assumptions, representations, and current project facts define the design problem?
2. **Execution:** Which actions may alter a candidate, through which versioned environment, and what counts as an observation or failure?
3. **Roles and methods:** Which components propose, predict, search, critique, repair, verify, or execute, and against which conventional alternative?
4. **Evidence:** Which bounded claim is under review, what comparator and check independence it requires, and who may reject or waive?
5. **Study decision:** What did the bounded study establish, fail to establish, or leave unresolved, and why did it stop?
6. **Feedback and transfer:** Which operating conditions permit automation, which later signals can reopen the result, and who owns that revalidation?
:::

As the next decision changes, so do the permitted automated actions, evidence checks, rollback paths, and decision rights. They should change with feedback latency, reversibility, and consequence. Assignment and answerability must survive those changes rather than being inferred anew at every tool or organizational boundary.

### Separating Fidelity from Authority

Evidence fidelity and decision authority remain separate. A proxy, cycle-level simulator, RTL test, emulator, synthesis flow, place-and-route result, or signoff check may support a claim within its scope. Stronger evidence does not grant a tool permission to approve a waiver or authorize tapeout. The evidence must fit the action, and the right to take that action must be assigned.

::: {.callout-war-story title="The Loophole in the Proxy"}
This is a composite scenario, not a single documented incident. A design team deploys an AI optimizer that achieves "perfect" timing closure on a critical block in record time. The agent had discovered and exploited a loophole in the fast, proxy Static Timing Analysis (STA) model used in the inner loop of the search. The block flawlessly passed the proxy constraints but immediately failed the human-owned signoff STA. This perfectly grounds why proxy evidence, however high the fidelity of the model that produced it, never equals signoff authority. The right to sign off requires the capacity to be held accountable for the final physical tapeout.
:::

## Enforcing the Epistemic Trust Boundary

An architecture study stays coherent only when it rigorously enforces this separation as the boundary between search and signoff. Work can move to a model, a script, or a specialist, but the responsibility for the resulting claim stays with a named architect. Few cases test this epistemic boundary as sharply as the public debate over AlphaChip, where a fast and capable placement method invites exactly the confusion the distinction is meant to prevent.

### Separating Search from Signoff

::: {.callout-war-story title="AlphaChip and the Ownership Boundary"}
- **The claim:** The public debate surrounding AlphaChip [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement], a reinforcement learning method for chip floorplanning, illustrates the separation between delegated work and assigned responsibility.

- **The gap:** It is tempting to credit the AI with designing the chip, which blurs the line between execution and architectural ownership. The agent generated candidate macro placements at superhuman speed, but it did not sign off on the physical limits of the silicon.

- **The lesson:** An RL agent can do the work of placement, but it does not own the responsibility for the final physical outcome. When independent reviewers debated the validity of the proxy metrics and the baseline comparisons, accountability fell on the human architects who defined the reward function, selected the benchmarks, and approved the final layouts for tapeout. The agent generated the floorplan; the architect owned the claim.
:::

Separate work from responsibility at the level of actual architecture artifacts. A multi-agent orchestration framework may deploy a team of specialized agents, such as a generator proposing a RISC-V core candidate, a critic debating its vector capabilities, and a verifier checking memory coherence, an organization of roles that recent RTL design systems make concrete [@WangEtAl2025RTLSquad]. This autonomous debate does not equal architectural signoff. The reason is not ceremony. Knight and Leveson showed that even independently developed program versions fail together on the same hard inputs (@sec-feedback-verification-trust), and a generator and a critic instantiated from the same foundation model start far behind that baseline, sharing training data, priors, and blind spots by construction. When the proposer and the challenger inherit the same misconception about a coherence corner case, their agreement is not two votes. It is one vote counted twice.

The same boundary governs humbler delegates. A script may synthesize the accelerator, a simulator may return power observations against the 3 W target, a validator may reject a malformed layout record, or a specialist may interpret a 3 nm domain constraint.

Delegating to a script often means encountering tool edge-cases and infrastructure failures.[^fn-eda-edge-cases-c11] None of those automated actions alone selects the XR workload, changes the power objective, recovers from the stalled run, expands the validity region, accepts a waiver, or makes the final architecture decision.

[^fn-eda-edge-cases-c11]: **Tool-path failures**: A script may hang for 72 hours on a FlexLM license checkout failure, or a 3-day simulation may die against a full disk. These are infrastructure noise, not evidence about the candidate.

### Inspectable Records of Assignment

@fig-architect-owned-boundary separates work that may be delegated from the responsibilities that must remain assigned. The upper band contains substantial technical work. The middle row contains instruments that make the work easier to inspect. The lower band remains visible across the entire study because no artifact, card, check, or replay package owns the resulting decision.

![**Delegated work and assigned responsibility.** Within a defined study, models, tools, checks, and specialists may assist formulation, exploration, implementation, evaluation, explanation, and defense. Named roles remain responsible for scope, abstraction, evidence standards, automation authority, exceptions and waivers, final approval, ownership transfer, and reopening.](images/F11a-architect-owned-boundary){#fig-architect-owned-boundary width="100%" fig-alt="Architecture study containing the six architecture capabilities, delegated assistance, an architectural claim for review, supporting instruments, and a full-width band of assigned responsibilities."}

The inspectable record that lets a reviewer challenge each assignment pairs every governing responsibility with the work that may be delegated and the artifact that proves it (@tbl-architect-responsibilities). Assignment does not mean that the same person performs the work, and it is not satisfied by naming an owner on a form. That owner must possess the authority, competence, and access needed to challenge the relevant record.

| **Assigned responsibility** | **Work that may be delegated** | **Inspectable record** |
|---|---|---|
| Define intent, workload, objective, comparator, constraints, and decision boundary | Retrieve precedents, enumerate candidate workloads, calculate metrics, draft a study brief | Bounded architecture question, selected workload and comparator, exclusions, decision owner |
| Approve represented knowledge and current state | Retrieve sources, form embeddings, summarize prior decisions, propose state updates, organize trajectories | Source and state versions, assumptions, missing fields, provenance, update decision, retirement or revalidation condition |
| Authorize actions and accept the execution contract | Generate candidates, call tools, translate formats, run checks, collect observations, retry declared failures | Action schema, candidate identity, environment and tool versions, artifacts, statuses, seeds, variance, cost, access boundary |
| Choose methods, components, roles, permissions, and review budget | Generate, predict, search, optimize, critique, repair, or verify within an assigned role | Role-to-component mapping, conventional alternative, prompt or configuration version where material, permissions, feedback and escalation budget, shared dependencies |
| Set the claim and evidence burden | Run matched comparisons, calculate results, prepare evidence packets, apply validated checks, flag contradictions | Claim, scope, baseline, observations, check independence, limitations, protected-review path, rejection or waiver record |
| Decide, stop, transfer, monitor, reopen, or retire | Summarize the record, propose next checks, prepare handoff and monitoring reports | Decision and rationale, failed alternatives, unresolved work, stopping reason, transfer package, monitoring trigger, new owner |

: **Delegation does not erase assignment.** Work can move among people, tools, and AI systems while the governing responsibilities remain attached to an explicit record. {#tbl-architect-responsibilities tbl-colwidths="[25,35,40]"}

::: {.callout-architect-checkpoint title="Check the delegation boundary"}
In the executed array study in @sec-executed-scale-study, a language model proposed a mapping and mechanism explanation, and a deterministic heuristic provided a conventional comparison. Validators and SCALE-Sim, a cycle-accurate systolic array simulator, rejected or returned observations under a frozen path. The authorized architect still had to accept the workload scope, separate the tie from the contradicted directional prediction, reject the unsupported mechanism explanation, record no change, and decide to stop.
:::

## Assigned Decision Rights

Because assigning responsibility requires naming who makes the final call, execution, acceptance, rejection, and waiver must be treated as distinct rights, not synonyms. A role permitted to execute a tool action need not be permitted to accept its result, and a reviewer allowed to reject a candidate need not be allowed to waive the failed check. A specialist may recommend a cross-layer change without owning the product decision. A review body may make the final decision while another role monitors later field evidence and initiates reopening.

These distinctions are not new. Human-factors engineering formalized the same progression decades ago as levels of automation, a ladder that runs from a system that merely offers alternatives to one that acts and informs only if asked [@ParasuramanEtAl2000LevelsAutomation]. The automotive industry then made that ladder contractual, with SAE J3016 assigning legally distinct responsibility at each level [@SAE2021J3016]. The decision rights in this chapter are rungs on the same ladder. Promoting a check from advisory to gating is a level transition, and the discipline the ladder adds is that every transition is a recorded decision with an owner rather than a default that hardens on its own.

### Governing Waivers

The waiver is the most dangerous of these rights, because it is the only one that authorizes proceeding against a failed check, so it must be a governed object rather than an escape hatch. A usable waiver names its scope, the specific check and candidate it covers rather than a blanket exemption. It names its owner, the role that accepted the residual risk. It names its expiration, the condition or date at which it lapses, and its revalidation trigger, the observation that reopens it early. And it leaves an audit trail, so a later reviewer can distinguish a considered exception from a habit. The failure mode this structure prevents is the permanent pass, a waiver granted once under schedule pressure that silently becomes part of the baseline. This failure mode has a name. Diane Vaughan, reconstructing the Challenger launch decision, called it the normalization of deviance [@Vaughan1996Challenger]. Each flight that survived a known O-ring anomaly became evidence that the anomaly was acceptable, until the waiver was no longer an exception anyone remembered granting. When a waiver outlives its stated scope, the check it silenced has effectively been deleted without anyone deciding to delete it, and an agentic loop accelerates that drift, because a waived check that stops firing disappears from the record faster than it ever did from a human review meeting.

### The Architect as Multi-Agent Economist

In a multi-agent system, specialist agents will inherently conflict as they ruthlessly optimize their proxy metrics. A Power Agent attempting to minimize dynamic switching activity will directly contradict a Performance Agent attempting to maximize speculative instruction issue. For the XR Lighthouse, this might manifest in the Network-on-Chip (NoC): a Power Agent might aggressively narrow NoC link widths to save dynamic power, accidentally starving the headset's real-time camera ingest of the massive bandwidth required for spatial tracking. The human architect owns the intent-to-metric translation and the Pareto negotiation between these agents. The architect acts as the "chief economist," resolving multi-agent deadlocks by aligning competing AI incentives with unquantifiable human product goals, such as user experience constraints or brand risk. An agent may find a mathematically optimal point on the Pareto frontier, but only the human architect can declare which point on that frontier represents the viable product.

::: {.callout-war-story title="The Turbo-Boost Power Loop"}
The failure to assign this Pareto negotiation to a human architect often leads to destructive system behavior. The following is a composite scenario, not a single documented incident. An automated power-management firmware loop conflicts with a hardware turbo-boost controller. Each acted as an independent agent optimizing its own proxy metric: one aggressively scaled down voltage to save power, while the other instantly spiked frequency in response to transient loads. Because no human architect explicitly owned the negotiation between these two control loops, the resulting destructive feedback loop caused sudden voltage droops and system crashes under specific workloads.
:::

### Agentic Conway's Law

The architect is no longer just designing the chip; they are designing the process that designs the chip. The human architect owns the agentic topology and workflow graph. Does the Verification Agent have immediate veto power over the Generator Agent, or do they debate in a peer-to-peer fashion? What is the sequence of escalation? The human architect essentially designs the "organizational chart" of the multi-agent system, recognizing an AI-era corollary to Conway's Law [@Conway1968Committees], the empirical regularity that a system's structure tends to mirror the communication structure of the organization that produced it. The final silicon tends to reflect the communication structures and assigned authorities of the AI agents that built it.

### Composing Judgments

This separation matters when work crosses hardware, software, package, and product boundaries. A compiler lead may own whether the current lowering path supports an instruction. A physical-design lead may own a congestion or power integrity rule. A product architect may own a workload or battery obligation. The architecture decision composes those judgments. The essential test is whether the combined assignments leave a gap, an unchallengeable waiver, or the problem of many hands, in which two roles each assume the other owns the transition [@Thompson1980ManyHands].

### Ownership Transfer

Ownership transfer is the transfer of an argument rather than just a report. Transferring ownership is more than passing a snapshot of RTL or a signoff artifact. The new owner needs the full context of the architecture, including architecture decision records, continuous integration pipeline logs, and design review minutes.

This context includes the dissent, the rejected alternatives, and the waivers. The new owner needs the causal chain of why the state is what it is, along with the conditions under which it remains valid. The transfer carries the claim, the represented knowledge, the candidate lineage, the method composition, the evidence, and the reopening conditions (@tbl-ownership-transfer).

| **Transfer object** | **Minimum content that must travel** | **Failure if omitted** |
|---|---|---|
| **Claim and current decision** | Bounded question, workload, objective, comparator, constraints, result, and decision status | Success or failure is repeated without knowing what was actually decided |
| **Knowledge and represented state** | Source and state versions, assumptions, omissions, expert judgments, update history, and known invalid regions | The new owner reasons from stale or incomplete premises |
| **Candidate and execution lineage** | Candidate identity, tool and environment versions, action history, artifacts, failures, seeds, variance, cost, and access limitations | The result cannot be replayed or linked to the evaluated artifact |
| **Method and role composition** | Components, assigned roles, permissions, material configuration versions, conventional alternative, shared dependencies, and escalation path | Later reviewers mistake one composition's result for a method-independent conclusion |
| **Evidence and exceptions** | Claim-to-observation link, baselines, check independence, limitations, counterevidence, rejects, waivers, protected-review status, and unresolved disputes | A bounded acceptance turns into an unqualified pass |
| **Monitoring and reopening** | Later signals, version mapping, rollback or mitigation condition, revalidation trigger, retirement rule, and newly assigned owner | Changed conditions leave an apparently permanent decision with no one able to reopen it |

: **Ownership transfer carries the argument.** A transfer is complete when the new role can locate the open obligations and knows what would invalidate or reopen the decision. {#tbl-ownership-transfer tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

A transfer can be proportional. A small reversible study need not produce a certification dossier, but it still must preserve enough state for the next authorized person to understand the decision, its limits, and the next obligation. A passing check on a component cannot by itself establish the behavior of the surrounding decision system across organizational interfaces.

The Pentium FDIV case in @sec-stronger-evaluation-expensive showed how a small omission became difficult and expensive to reverse after shipment. The ownership question is different but no less concrete. In the FDIV case, the assumptions made by algorithm experts regarding table optimizations were not explicitly transferred as testable obligations to the validation teams, leaving a critical verification gap. At each consequential transition, someone had to own the evidence standard, unresolved exceptions, and authority to proceed, and after a transfer the next role also needed the assumptions and open conditions that could still overturn the decision. The public record does not reconstruct every internal handoff, so the case marks where a sound process must assign that responsibility at its technical, product, and public transitions.

::: {.callout-war-story title="The Lost Context of the Thermal Model"}
The following composite scenario, not a single documented incident, highlights the same gap in ownership transfer. An ML-based thermal prediction model is trained and transferred to a physical design team for use in placement optimization. However, the tacit assumption that *aggressive clock-gating would be enabled* across the SoC failed to transfer. The physical design team used the model to place macros tightly, assuming the model accounted for worst-case thermals. The resulting silicon suffered massive thermal throttling in the field because the environment constraints that made the model's predictions valid did not travel with the artifact.
:::

### When the Design Fails in the Field

Ownership transfer has a final test that arrives uninvited. When a shipped design fails in the field, the loop that produced it runs one more time, under time pressure and in public, and every right this chapter names is exercised at once. Someone must own detection, deciding that scattered telemetry is an incident rather than noise. Someone must own containment and the rollback or mitigation it requires, using the reversibility that @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack priced. Someone must own disclosure, deciding what customers and partners are told while the root cause is still a hypothesis. Someone must own the root-cause study itself, which is a bounded architecture study like any other, with the failing silicon as its ground truth. And someone must own the reopen decision: which committed claims the incident invalidates, which studies must rerun, and which waivers no longer hold. Organizations rehearse none of this if the rights exist only as table rows. The FDIV and thermal-model cases above are what the unrehearsed version looks like.

Containment is only a real right when the lever it needs was built before tapeout. Architects have always priced their own verification gaps into the silicon. A feature the schedule did not allow to be fully verified ships behind a chicken bit, a configuration register that can turn it off in the field, and the errata-and-stepping pipeline exists so that containment has a channel before anyone knows what will need containing. The rule for the agentic loop is the same one the FDIV aftermath taught. Whoever signs off on a capability the evidence chain did not fully cover owns the obligation to ship the lever that disables it, because containment authority without a designed-in mitigation path is a table row, not a right.

## Making Tacit Knowledge Reviewable

Making this responsibility reviewable is challenged by an institutional problem known as the irony of automation [@Bainbridge1983Ironies]. The drive to delegate routine work removes the practice through which experts once learned to detect unusual failures. If an AI flawlessly generates memory controller configurations or handles coherence protocol verification, junior architects never develop the tacit knowledge to recognize subtle DRAM scheduling collisions unique to XR streaming frame buffers, or to spot a congested routing channel and a subtle race condition.

### Retaining the Feel for What Checks Miss

This tacit knowledge includes the implicit assumptions about physical constraints, tool behaviors, and system boundary conditions that keep the system stable. An organization that cannot identify someone who retains this tacit feel for what a check establishes, what it misses, and when it should be challenged cannot responsibly grant that check broad authority. Preserving that feel requires deliberately rotating experts through hands-on studies rather than naming an owner.

Formal records solve only part of the transfer problem. Architecture decisions also depend on tacit knowledge [@Polanyi1966TacitDimension], which encompasses the undocumented constraints and context that experienced engineers carry.[^fn-cross-layer-exceptions-c11]

[^fn-cross-layer-exceptions-c11]: **Tacit constraints (examples)**: A packaging engineer may know that a chiplet partition or an AI-proposed macro placement for the Lighthouse SoC might pass logical checks but structurally compromise the 3\ nm package's physical power-delivery mesh, a compiler lead that the current LLVM backend cannot efficiently lower a proposed vector instruction, and a senior architect that the accelerator's coherency traffic will starve the display controller under the 3\ W TDP target.

Not every judgment can be fully encoded into a schema. Enough of a consequential judgment must be exposed for another person to understand where it came from, where it applies, who validated it, and when it needs another review.

### Constraint Elicitation

A disciplined elicitation-and-validation process helps make tacit knowledge reviewable (@fig-tacit-extraction-bridge). A model or reviewer may locate, compare, summarize, or elicit relevant judgments from prior reviews, waivers, reports, source code, and domain experts. A named domain owner then validates the interpretation, scope, and consequences. The validated part becomes a sourced project-state entry, an environment constraint, a rejection check, a protected note, or a qualified judgment that remains explicitly human.

![**Reviewing tacit knowledge before using it.** A model can help elicit and organize domain knowledge, but a named domain expert must validate constraints, assumptions, and rejection conditions. Conflicts, expiration, or new evidence require another review rather than a silent overwrite.](images/F11b-tacit-extraction-bridge){#fig-tacit-extraction-bridge width="100%" fig-alt="Diagram showing domain knowledge passing through AI-assisted elicitation and domain validation before entering represented study state, with conflict, expiration, and new evidence returning the record for revalidation."}

Every retained judgment should expose four elements, specifically its source, scope, owner, and revalidation condition. A constraint tied to one LLVM revision, process design kit, workload mix, or approved waiver cannot silently become a permanent rule. The architect answerable for the larger decision need not perform every specialist task, but must know which judgments can change the result, who validated them, and how they will be revisited.

## Common Objections

Making judgment reviewable sounds expensive, and treated as paperwork it can create false confidence. The objections below each have a direct answer.

### Process Objections

- **"This overformalizes ordinary architecture work":** The record should be proportional to consequence, reversibility, interface span, evidence weakness, and transfer needs. A local, reversible exploration may need a small study card and replay path. A cross-interface exception or difficult-to-reverse decision needs more. The framework inherits recognizable practices from design-space exploration, multifidelity evaluation, and engineering review; it does not require every study to mimic an aviation safety case.

- **"AI may add no value":** This is a possible and useful result. In the executed @sec-running-the-loop study, the model tied the deterministic heuristic, offered a contradicted directional prediction, and gave an unsupported mechanism explanation under one frozen path. The architecture outcome was no change, and the study stopped. A framework that cannot preserve this result without converting it into an AI success claim will misreport a null result as progress.

- **"Assignment slows experts and validated automation":** Validated routine checks may reject candidates or advance bounded transitions without convening a broad review every time. Human attention should concentrate on changed scope, weak or protected evidence, exceptions, cross-layer effects, correlated failures, difficult-to-reverse consequences, and ownership transfer. The organization still owns the validation, audit, and escalation boundary of the routine check. For example, a deterministic equivalence checker may be assigned the authority to automatically approve layout modifications if they do not alter logic, but the organization still owns the decision to grant that tool this authority and the duty to periodically audit it.

- **"Naming an owner creates false confidence":** Assignment does not make a decision correct. It creates an authorized challenge path and prevents responsibility from disappearing between tools, teams, or lifecycle stages. An owner without access, competence, or authority is an unfilled role, not a completed assignment.

- **"Protected evidence cannot be made fully inspectable":** Authorized protected review can support an internal decision when the reviewer can inspect and challenge the material. Public claims must remain within the public or independently audited record. Confidentiality does not turn an inaccessible assertion into public evidence.

- **"Human authority only reflects current model limits":** The technical boundary may move, but broader machine authority still requires someone to define its scope, validated failure behavior, audit path, exception handling, and authorization. If future systems can assume some of those judgments, the chapter's decision-right distinctions remain useful for stating exactly what moved.

### The Moral Crumple Zone

- **"The named owner is just a liability sponge":** A person held answerable for decisions they cannot actually supervise becomes a moral crumple zone, absorbing blame for failures the surrounding automation produced [@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones]. The danger is real precisely when automation runs faster and at higher volume than any person can follow. When agents generate and filter thousands of candidates overnight, human operators lose the situational awareness that oversight assumes [@ParasuramanRiley1997HumansAutomation].

A signature is not a capacity check. An owner without the access, time, and independent competence to detect and stop the failures they nominally own is an unfilled role, and naming one changes nothing [@Green2022HumanOversight]. This is why the assignment tests later in this chapter ask who owns a decision and whether that owner could actually have caught the failure.

Capacity is necessary but not sufficient, and its failure mode is not only the crumple zone. A reviewer with every needed qualification can still exhibit automation bias, the documented tendency to accept an automated recommendation even when the raw evidence contradicts it [@SkitkaEtAl1999AutomationBias]. This is an error of commission by a capable owner, not the misassigned blame that falls on an owner who never could have supervised. The countermeasure is procedural rather than motivational. Have the reviewer commit a position from the evidence before the agent's recommendation is revealed, the same reason signoff STA derives its timing independently instead of trusting the optimizer's own report. A review process that shows the recommendation first has already spent most of its independence.

Not every architecture problem needs AI, a multi-agent system, a formal loop, or a full study packet. The discipline is to make the claim, scope, evidence, decision, and responsibility proportionate and challengeable when consequential work is delegated.

## Maintaining Shared Infrastructure

Achieving this proportionality depends on maintained resources, which directly addresses three of the field's challenges, namely the dataset crisis [@GebruEtAl2021Datasheets], the tools infrastructure gap, and reproducibility [@PineauEtAl2021Reproducibility]. Without versioned state, executable environments, checks, and replay records, every team must reconstruct the conditions of a decision from memory, exacerbating the reproducibility crisis. The organization must own more than access to models and tools to bridge the tools infrastructure gap.

### The System of Record

It needs a maintained chain from knowledge to execution to evidence to later feedback, overcoming the dataset crisis by treating its own execution history as a curated corporate asset. Shared infrastructure is the system of record, not just a platform to make AI faster. Its primary purpose is to ensure that when an architecture decision is questioned, the exact state, prompt, toolchain, and context that led to it are reproducible within the limits of vendor IP, tool versions, and license availability. This creates a continuous learning requirement. A model frozen at tapeout does not decay on its own, but its validity against evolving PDKs and compiler stacks does; the moat is not the model itself, but the infrastructure to continually fine-tune and align it on the latest silicon telemetry.

Every shared architecture resource needs a named owner, a maintenance decision, and a stated failure mode for when it goes stale or unreviewable (@tbl-field-maintenance).

| **Shared architecture resource** | **What it preserves** | **Required owner and maintenance decision** | **Failure if neglected** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Knowledge corpora, datasets, embeddings, representations, and project trajectories | Sources, design distinctions, prior decisions, failed regions, and current state used in @sec-data-representations-world-models | A qualified owner approves inclusion and update destinations, records source and objective, tests whether important architecture distinctions remain recoverable, and retires stale material | Retrieval or prediction appears current while omitting the state or distinction on which the decision depends |
| Executable environments, action contracts, tool interfaces, candidate lineage, and artifacts | The exact path by which actions changed a candidate and tools returned observations in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces | Environment and tool owners maintain versions, access, failure semantics, replayability, and identity across translations | License and environment bit-rot prevents reproduction, a retry silently changes the path, or the evaluated artifact cannot be linked to the candidate |
| Method, component, and role configurations with matched conventional baselines | The composition that generated, predicted, searched, critiqued, repaired, or verified in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization | A study or platform owner records the component-role mapping, material configuration versions, permissions, shared dependencies, feedback budget, and comparator | Improvement is attributed to "AI" without knowing which role, composition, cost, or conventional alternative produced it |
| Claims, observations, checks, counterevidence, disputes, waivers, and protected-review paths | The bounded reasoning that turns observations into support, non-support, or unresolved evidence in @sec-feedback-verification-trust | A claim or review owner maintains scope, check independence, access, exception expiration, and reopening conditions | Passing one check becomes universal evidence, a protected assertion becomes a public claim, or a waiver becomes a permanent pass |
| Executed-study packages, negative results, stopping reasons, and replay manifests | What was actually run, learned, rejected, left unresolved, and decided in @sec-running-the-loop | The decision owner accepts the result, preserves material failed paths, and decides whether replay is possible or only partial | Teams rerun dead ends, inflate a no-change result, or cannot distinguish executed behavior from a plan |
| Later field and software-enablement feedback linked to system and submission versions | Evidence on the deployed hardware-software pair and signals that may reopen a decision in @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack | Lifecycle owners maintain version mapping, attribution alternatives, monitoring, rollback or mitigation triggers, revalidation, and retirement | Later gains or failures are assigned to the wrong cause, or stale design evidence survives a changed workload or stack |

: **Unmaintained infrastructure silently corrupts every later decision.** The discipline needs linked resources that connect a question and representation to tools, feedback, evidence, challenge, and lifecycle ownership. {#tbl-field-maintenance tbl-colwidths="[20,20,30,30]"}

### Provenance Boundaries

Keep three access modes distinct:

1. **Public comparison:** supports public claims only within material others can inspect or reproduce.
2. **Protected inspection:** permits authorized technical challenge without making the underlying artifact public.
3. **Replay:** reconstructs an executed path when dependencies and access allow; it is not synonymous with public release or independent evidence.

These resources come from public benchmarks, open tools, research artifacts, industrial reviews, telemetry, and synthetic tasks, but an undifferentiated log is not a dataset. A reusable architecture record connects the question, state, action, observation, failed alternatives, interpretation, decision, and later update. The resource may be a corpus, trajectory, embedding, tool environment, evidence packet, or protected archive, but its value comes from preserving those relations and their scope.

Embeddings and learned representations require special discipline. Record their source material, version, objective, and evaluation of whether decision-relevant architecture distinctions remain recoverable. Do not treat them as timeless, neutral infrastructure.

Provenance is also a hard intellectual property (IP) boundary. When using external models or shared infrastructure, architects must track the exact lineage of generated candidates. If an AI proposes a specialized accelerator block, the organization must be able to prove it was generated from authorized sources, not hallucinated from a competitor's proprietary datasheet. Without strict IP provenance, a technically brilliant design may be legally unusable. This raises a critical interoperability challenge. Proprietary, encrypted PDKs and closed-source commercial EDA APIs inherently resist the massive, automated data scraping and large-scale pretraining that enabled the software AI revolution.

The hardest ownership question crosses company boundaries. A single study may depend on a vendor's foundation model, another vendor's licensed IP macro, a foundry's encrypted PDK, and a commercial EDA tool, and no architect inside the integrating organization can inspect any of them. Responsibility does not dilute across this supply chain. The organization that commits the design owns the consequence, whatever recourse its contracts allocate afterward. What the architect can own is the boundary record: which external component each claim depends on, which vendor attestations stand in for inspection, and which failures would be undiagnosable in house. A dependency whose failure could not even be diagnosed internally is a risk decision, and it deserves to be recorded as one.

## Building Team Competence

Yet infrastructure does not maintain or challenge itself. Competence requires the ability to build and challenge the entire argument chain as a team, rather than relying on prompt fluency, universal tool mastery, or ceremonial approval. An architect should be able to formulate a bounded question, identify missing state, trace candidate lineage, ask why a method fits the task, separate observation from evidence, challenge exceptions, and reclassify the next decision. Deep specialists remain necessary, and they bear the responsibility of making the tool, model, dataset, assumption, failure mode, and uncertainty legible at the architecture boundary.

### The Bounded Study Exercise

A team does not need to build the field's entire infrastructure before it can begin. It needs one bounded architecture question and one challengeable study. The initial record should contain:

1. **Study Scope:** decision, workload scope, objective, comparator, and baseline;
2. **State Representation:** knowledge sources, represented state, assumptions, and missing fields;
3. **Execution Trace:** candidate identity, actions, environment, tool path, observations, failures, versions, and costs;
4. **Method Roles:** model or algorithm roles, permissions, matched conventional alternative, and review budget;
5. **Evidence Burden:** claim, evidence burden, check independence, counterevidence, and protected access where applicable;
6. **Decision Status:** no-change, rejection, waiver, recommendation, stopping, and replay status;
7. **Role Assignment:** roles allowed to propose, execute, reject, waive, recommend, decide, monitor, reopen, and retire; and
8. **Revalidation Triggers:** the later feedback or changed condition that would require revalidation.

A good exercise may end with no architecture change, a failed tool path, or no measurable AI contribution. The observable competence is in diagnosing and recording the result correctly, not in producing a positive result. Competence should be tested on an unfamiliar but tractable architecture problem. Classic quantitative architecture remains the grounding discipline.

### The Progression of Competence

The progression in @tbl-team-competence treats the unfamiliar bounded problem as an internal onboarding, qualification, or team-review exercise whose work products can be challenged by another architect.

| **Stage** | **Observable performance** |
|---|---|
| **Begin** | Execute and replay one bounded study; distinguish action, observation, evidence, and decision; document one failure fully. |
| **Develop** | Compare method and role choices, audit a proxy or check, diagnose a cross-layer omission, and transfer a study with its open obligations. |
| **Lead** | Set evidence and authority boundaries across teams, maintain shared infrastructure, rule on exceptions, and reopen or retire claims as conditions change. |

: **Competence appears in the work.** A team demonstrates Architecture 2.0 by completing and defending bounded architecture studies across methods and lifecycles. {#tbl-team-competence tbl-colwidths="[20,80]"}

Teams need enough direct contact with tools, failures, and cross-layer effects to supervise the work they delegate. This continued practice is what answers the irony of automation raised earlier, because retained expertise requires ongoing hands-on work rather than a designation on a form. Education cannot stop at prompting, and expert practice cannot stop at final approval.

## Open Research Questions

Even with strong team competence, as the marginal cost of searching the architectural state space falls, the architect's role continues to shift from exploration toward defining constraints and signing off on results. Three problems remain open.

**Theme 1: AI-Native Hardware Abstractions.** Today's HDLs and ISAs were built for human designers, not for learned methods to optimize directly.

- Can hardware description languages and ISAs expose a differentiable search space that learned methods optimize directly, and what is lost when they do?
- Can compositional microarchitectural primitives let neural networks assemble and optimize data paths directly, rather than through RTL syntax?

**Theme 2: The Limits of ML vs. Formal Logic.** Some architectural properties can be formally proven; others admit only statistical evidence.

- Can neuro-symbolic[^fn-neuro-symbolic-c11] agents partition architectural design spaces, shifting between neural search for topology generation and SMT solvers for invariant verification?

[^fn-neuro-symbolic-c11]: **Neuro-symbolic methods**: Hybrid systems that pair neural networks, which search and generalize from data, with symbolic engines such as satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers, which prove or refute exact logical properties. Each side covers the failure mode of the other [@GarcezLamb2023Neurosymbolic].

- Which architectural properties, such as memory coherence or protocol deadlock freedom, admit formal invariant proofs, and which admit only statistical evidence, so a study can route each claim to the check that can actually settle it?
- What evidence about a check's scope, failure behavior, and audit path justifies promoting it from an advisory signal to a gating one, and can that authority be revoked automatically when conditions drift?

**Theme 3: The Cognitive Verification Gap.** When search costs almost nothing, the human reviewer becomes the real bottleneck.

- When exploration cost falls to near zero, human review becomes the binding constraint [@BowmanEtAl2022ScalableOversight]. What review tooling and sampling lets a bounded human budget cover an unbounded candidate stream, and can a stronger generator be trained to produce outputs a smaller, time-limited verifier can still check [@KirchnerEtAl2024ProverVerifier]?
- Can we design and measure a genuine capacity check that verifies an accountable owner had the access, time, and competence to catch a failure, rather than treating a signature as oversight and turning that owner into a moral crumple zone?
- How can an organization keep enough hands-on expertise to make oversight meaningful once routine studies are automated, the irony of automation, and how would we measure that a reviewer's feel for what a check misses remains current?

That closes the last of these sections, and it is worth saying what they are not. The questions collected across these chapters are not a research agenda, and they are not complete. They are the places where this book's argument stopped being able to answer its own questions, written down rather than smoothed over. Some will look answered within a few years, and others will turn out to have been the wrong question. A reader who finishes with a sharper set of their own has taken the right thing from them.

## Returning to the Architecture Question

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Inalienable Ownership of the Physical Result"}
You can delegate the traversal of the design space, but you cannot delegate the responsibility for the silicon. The human architect owns the formulation of the question, the selection of the baselines, the rigor of the evaluation constraints, and the final physical consequence of the implemented design.
:::


A model or composed system may help formulate a study, propose candidates, execute tools, and detect contradictions, but it does not thereby select its own workload scope, waive an independent check, or authorize a difficult-to-reverse architecture transition.

### The Division of Labor

This division of labor reinforces the epistemic trust boundary (@sec-feedback-verification-trust), the line between search and signoff. AI may propose RTL or architectural parameters, but the optimizer under evaluation must not set or edit the criteria that judge it, whether that means the signoff verification testbenches, the foundry-owned physical rule decks that no one alters, or the timing constraints a human engineer maintains. Because optimization algorithms will exploit any loophole in a scoring metric, the human architect keeps authority over the evaluation criteria. If an AI generates a passing result for a flawed proxy metric, the resulting timing violation or thermal failure belongs to the architect. They must ensure the metrics used by models strictly align with physical reality, and recognize that foundational standard-cell libraries and IP macros ultimately dictate the PPA ceiling of any AI-generated design.

### The Architecture 2.0 Thesis

This is the book's culminating thesis, and it closes the claim the preface opened. The design loop is now part of the architecture. Across these chapters it acquired a specification, the bounded claim; state, actions, and feedback paths; performance metrics in the feedback budget; verification obligations in the evidence chain; and characteristic failure modes, from proxy gaming to silent drift. The loop diagram this book opened with is no longer an illustration. It is a bill of materials. Architecture 2.0 is not AI designing chips; it is architects engineering the loop that designs alongside them, bounding the search, defining the evaluation, and owning the result rather than dictating every keystroke or tool invocation. Enforcing the epistemic trust boundary means ensuring that:

- **Questions are explicit:** the architecture question and comparator are explicit;
- **State is grounded:** the represented state is sourced, scoped, and current enough for the claim;
- **Traceability is preserved:** the executed candidate and tool path are identifiable;
- **Roles are fair:** the method and role composition fit the task and are compared fairly;
- **Evidence is bounded:** observations become evidence only through a bounded review;
- **Outcomes are visible:** rejection, waiver, stopping, and no-change outcomes remain visible;
- **Feedback reopens claims:** later feedback reopens the result when its scope no longer transfers; and
- **Ownership is assigned:** each decision right and open obligation has a qualified, authorized owner.

::: {.callout-architect-checkpoint title="Test the assignment"}
- **Assignment test.** Can a reviewer identify who set scope, authorized automated actions, judged evidence sufficiency, approved any exception, and made the final decision?
- **Capacity test.** Given the named owner's real access, time, and the volume of automated decisions they nominally supervise, could they have detected and prevented the failure, or have we named an owner structurally unable to exercise the responsibility?
- **Transfer test.** Can the next owner find unresolved claims, assumptions, rejected alternatives, waivers, relevant versions, monitoring conditions, and reopening triggers?
- **Challenge test.** Can a qualified person dispute the evidence or interpretation and reach the role authorized to respond?
:::

@sec-running-the-loop shows how to begin with one bounded setup, @sec-architecture-20-ontology supplies the compact study card, and @sec-appendix-a-reviewer-checklist gives reviewers a checklist for judging AI-assisted architecture claims.

Architecture 2.0 succeeds not when an AI system emits a design, but when another architect can understand what was decided, challenge why the evidence supports it, identify who held each consequential right, and know what would reopen the decision. That reviewable ownership is what lets the field accumulate defensible architecture decisions and better designs rather than isolated model outputs.
